Training Program: Civil Construction
Subject: Scaffolding
Introduction
Frame scaffolds are widely used in construction because they are versatile, economical, and easy to assemble. But their safety depends on more than simply putting the components together. Proper erection, secure assembly, and a thorough inspection are essential before the scaffold is put into service.
In this module, you will learn how to:
Prepare a stable scaffold base.
Assemble and secure the frame structure.
Provide safe access and fall protection.
Check the platform and scaffold stability.
Identify electrical hazards.
Inspect the scaffold before it is used.
Interaction:
Animated scaffold builds from the foundation upward.
Start with the Foundation
On-screen
A stable scaffold starts with a firm foundation.
A supported scaffold must be set on:
Base plates
Mud sills
Or another adequate firm foundation
The footing must support the loaded scaffold without settling or displacement.

Never use unstable objects to support a scaffold.
Voice-over
Before erecting the scaffold, check the ground and foundation.
The scaffold must be supported by a base plate, mud sill, or another adequate firm foundation.
The footing must be capable of supporting the loaded scaffold without settling or displacement.
Unstable objects must not be used to support scaffolds or platform units.
Interaction — Choose the Safe Base
Show three options:
A: Base plates on firm mud sillsB: Frames on unstable blocksC: Frames on loose scrap material
Select the safe foundation.
Correct answer: A
3. Keep the Structure Stable
Screen 3 — Keep the Scaffold Plumb and Braced
On-screen
During erection, make sure the scaffold is:
PlumbLevelSquareProperly braced
Supported scaffold frames and uprights must be plumb and braced to prevent swaying and displacement.
Voice-over
A stable base is only the beginning.
As the scaffold is erected, frames and uprights must remain plumb and properly braced.

Using a level during assembly can help ensure that the structure remains properly aligned.
Visual:Show a scaffold first leaning, then corrected to a plumb position.

4. Build the Support Structure
Connect and Brace the Frames
On-screen
Frames and panels must be connected using:
Cross braces
Horizontal braces
Diagonal braces
The braces secure the vertical members laterally.
All brace connections must be secured against dislodging.
Voice-over
Frames and panels must be connected by cross, horizontal, or diagonal braces, alone or in combination.
As frames are stacked, the braces must keep the scaffold plumb, level, and square.
Brace connections must be secured to prevent them from becoming dislodged.
Interaction
Build the scaffold correctly.
The learner clicks:
Frame → Brace → Secure connection → Next frame

5. Secure the Frames
Screen 5 — Prevent Separation and Uplift
On-screen
Frames and panels must be joined vertically using:
Coupling pinsStacking pinsOr equivalent means
Where uplift can occur, frames must be locked together.
Voice-over
Frames and panels must be joined vertically using coupling or stacking pins, or equivalent means.
They must also be locked together to prevent uplift where uplift can occur.
Uplift is the separation of one frame from the frame below it. It can occur because of high winds, climbing end frames, overloading, or impact from tools and materials.
Interaction — Spot the Problem
Show two frames:
A: Properly pinnedB: Upper frame separated
Question:What hazard is shown in option B?
Answer: Uplift

6. Check the Scaffold Capacity
Screen 6 — Respect the Load Capacity
On-screen
The scaffold must support:
Its own weight + at least 4 × the maximum intended load
Do not overload the scaffold.
Never remove braces because they are "in the way."
Voice-over
Scaffolds and scaffold components must be capable of supporting their own weight and at least four times their maximum intended load without failure.
Removing braces can redistribute the load to fewer structural members and can contribute to overloading.
Braces must not be removed while work is being performed on the scaffold.

7. Provide Safe Access
Screen 7 — Access the Scaffold Safely
On-screen
Workers must have safe access to scaffold levels.
Remember:
Never climb cross-braces as a means of access.
Portable, hook-on, and attachable ladders must be positioned so they do not tip the scaffold.
Voice-over
Workers are particularly vulnerable to falls when climbing onto or off a scaffold.
Employees must be able to safely access scaffold levels that are two feet above or below an access point.
OSHA specifically prohibits using cross-braces as a means of access.
Interaction
Show:
Proper ladder
Access frame
Cross-brace
Which one should never be used for access?
Correct: Cross-brace

8. Fall Protection
Screen 8 — Protect Workers from Falls
On-screen
Fall protection is required when a scaffold is:
10 feet or more above a lower level.
Fall protection consists of:
Guardrail SystemsORPersonal Fall Arrest Systems
Voice-over
Falls are the number one scaffold hazard.
Each employee working on a scaffold more than 10 feet above a lower level must be protected from falling to that lower level.
OSHA allows the required fall protection to consist of a guardrail system or a personal fall arrest system meeting the applicable requirements.
Visual
Worker on scaffold → 10 ft. indicator → guardrail appears.

9. Check the Guardrails
Screen 9 — Inspect the Guardrail System
On-screen
Before releasing the scaffold for use, check that guardrail systems are properly installed along the open sides and ends of platforms.
For supported scaffolds:
Toprail: 36–45 inchesMinimum top edge for scaffolds manufactured or placed in service after Jan. 1, 2000: 38 inches
Midrail: Approximately midway between the toprail and platform.
Voice-over
Guardrail systems must be installed along the open sides and ends of platforms before the scaffold is released for use by employees other than erection and dismantling crews.
The top edge of toprails on supported scaffolds must generally be between 36 and 45 inches above the platform. For scaffolds manufactured or placed in service after January 1, 2000, the minimum top edge height is 38 inches.
Interaction:Click the Toprail, Midrail, and Platform.

10. Check the Platform
Screen 10 — Inspect the Working Platform
On-screen
Before use, check that the platform is:
Fully planked or decked
Also check for:
Unsafe gaps
Displaced planks
Unsecured platform components
Unsafe working conditions
Voice-over
The platform is the main work area of the scaffold, so it must be inspected carefully.
Each platform must be fully planked or decked between the front uprights and guardrail supports.
Gaps greater than one inch are generally not permitted between adjacent planks or deck units, or between the platform and uprights, unless a wider space is necessary under the applicable requirements. In such cases, the gap must be as small as possible and must not exceed 9½ inches.

11. Keep the Scaffold Upright
Screen 11 — Check Scaffold Stability
On-screen
4:1 Height-to-Base Ratio
When a supported scaffold exceeds the applicable 4:1 height-to-base ratio, it must be restrained against tipping.
Use:
Guys • Ties • Braces
Voice-over
A supported scaffold must be restrained from tipping when its height exceeds four times its minimum base dimension.
Guys, ties, or braces are used to provide the required restraint.
Interaction
Show two scaffolds:
Safe ratioExceeds 4:1
The learner identifies which scaffold requires additional restraint.

12. Electrical Hazards
Screen 12 — Maintain Electrical Clearance
On-screen
Keep the scaffold away from overhead power lines.
General rule: 10 feet
For insulated power lines of less than 300 volts:
3 feet
When work requires closer proximity, applicable protective measures must be taken.
Voice-over
Because scaffolds are often made of metal, contact with overhead power lines can result in serious injury or death.
Maintain the required clearance from power lines and take the appropriate precautions when work must be performed closer to the lines.
Interaction — Identify the Hazard
Show a scaffold approaching an overhead power line.
The learner identifies the unsafe condition.

13. Personnel and Competent Person
Screen 13 — Who Can Make Safety Decisions?
On-screen
Competent Person
The Competent Person has an important role in scaffold safety.
The Competent Person supervises or makes required safety determinations related to scaffold erection, alteration, access, fall protection, and inspection.
Voice-over
Scaffolds may only be altered under the supervision and direction of a Competent Person.
The Competent Person is also responsible for determining the feasibility and safety of providing safe access and fall protection for employees involved in scaffold erection or dismantling, where required.

14. Pre-Use Inspection
Screen 14 — Inspect Before Every Shift
On-screen
Before each work shift:
A Competent Person must inspect the scaffold for visible defects.
An additional inspection is required after any occurrence that could affect the scaffold's structural integrity.
Check:
✓ Foundation✓ Frames & braces✓ Pins & connections✓ Access✓ Fall protection✓ Platform✓ Stability✓ Electrical hazards
Voice-over
A scaffold must not be considered ready for use simply because erection is complete.
The scaffold and its components must be inspected for visible defects before each work shift by a Competent Person.
An additional inspection is required after an occurrence that could affect the scaffold's structural integrity.

15. Inspection Scenario
Screen 15 — Is This Scaffold Ready?
Scenario
You are the Competent Person conducting the pre-shift inspection.
You notice:
A missing brace.
An unsecured platform.
A worker using a cross-brace for access.
A scaffold that exceeds the applicable height-to-base ratio without required restraint.
An overhead power line too close to the scaffold.
Task
Identify every condition that must be corrected before the scaffold is released for use.
Interaction:Learner clicks the hazards directly on the scaffold.
Feedback
Correct.
Each unsafe condition must be addressed before the scaffold is used.

16. Knowledge Check
Question 1
A scaffold is more than 10 feet above a lower level.
What must be provided?
A. Additional platform boardsB. Fall protectionC. A second ladderD. Additional workers
Correct Answer: B

Question 2
Which of the following is prohibited as a means of scaffold access?
A. Portable ladderB. Hook-on ladderC. Proper access frameD. Cross-brace
Correct Answer: D

Question 3
What is the purpose of coupling or stacking pins?
A. To increase platform widthB. To join frames verticallyC. To provide electrical groundingD. To support workers
Correct Answer: B

Question 4
Who must inspect the scaffold for visible defects before each work shift?
A. Any workerB. The project administratorC. A Competent PersonD. The material supplier
Correct Answer: C

17. Final Inspection Checklist
Before You Step Onto the Scaffold
01 — Foundation
Firm and adequate
02 — Structure
Plumb, level, braced, and securely connected
03 — Connections
Frames properly joined and protected against uplift where required
04 — Access
Safe access provided
05 — Fall Protection
Required protection in place
06 — Platform
Fully planked/decked and safe for work
07 — Stability
Properly restrained when required
08 — Electrical Safety
Required clearance maintained
09 — Inspection
Completed by a Competent Person

18. Closing
Safe Erection. Thorough Inspection. Safe Work.
A safe frame scaffold depends on two things:
Build It Right.
Check It Before Use.
Always follow the applicable OSHA requirements, the scaffold manufacturer's instructions, and your employer's safety procedures.
Never assume a scaffold is safe because it looks complete.
